div.head: I As 4.1[Ld]
div.ab: Se godcunde lare us gemynaþ, þæt we ða heofonlica ðinga mid ðam eorþlicum ⁊ ða ecelic mid ðam hwilwendlicum geearniaþ.
Hortatur nos sermo diuinus eterna cum terrenis, celestia cum caducis promereri.
[Se godcunde lare us gemynaþ, þæt we ða heofonlica ðinga mid ðam eorþlicum ⁊ ða ecelic mid ðam hwilwendlicum geearniaþ.]
(Die göttliche Lehre ermahnt uns, dass wir die himmlischen Dinge durch die irdischen und die ewigen durch die zeitlichen verdienen lq.)
(The divine teaching exhorts us that we earn heavenly things through earthly ones and eternal things through temporal ones, lq.)
For the divine teaching instructs us that we gain the things of heaven by those of the earth, and the eternal by the temporal.
div.note: Only in Ld and Quadripartitus; not in D or G.

note.seg: Der Satz reiht sich zwar besser 3 an, wie ihn Ld bietet; allein 4 ist offenbar archetyp. So scheint mir 4, 1 dem Bearbeiter lq zu gehören
The sentence, as Ld gives it, does indeed follow better on 3; but 4 evidently belongs to the archetype. 4, 1 therefore seems to me to belong to the redactor lq

Der Gedanke (vgl. Gl Himmel 4) kehrt in Urkk., auch Æthelstans, häufig wieder: mercanda sunt æterna caducis a. 937 Bi 721; mid þam gewytendlicum madmum þa unaleori endlican madmas begitan sceolde a. 932 Bi 693. Schon Ælfred versteht Augustins Worte Deus, per quem discimus, aliena esse quae aliquando nostra, et nostra quae aliquando aliena putabamus als weoruldwela im Ggs. zu heofonrice; ed. Hargrove p. 7

The idea (cf. Gl Himmel 4) recurs frequently in charters, Æthelstan’s among them: mercanda sunt æterna caducis a. 937 Bi 721; mid þam gewytendlicum madmum þa unaleori endlican madmas begitan sceolde a. 932 Bi 693. Ælfred already understands Augustine’s words Deus, per quem discimus, aliena esse quae aliquando nostra, et nostra quae aliquando aliena putabamus as weoruldwela in contrast to heofonrice; ed. Hargrove p. 7
